extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how researchers and reviewers should treat and practice peer review within science, emphasizing humility, openness, and evidence-based evaluation rather than deference to institutional gatekeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review is fallible / not the gold standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is a recent, fallible institution introduced long after the scientific revolution and standardized only after Einstein's most productive era; it has historically failed to recognize groundbreaking work (e.g., Siler et al. (2014) showing focal journals rejected many highly cited manuscripts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume peer review guarantees correctness or that acceptance equals truth; be aware of historical failures and systemic limitations when evaluating research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat peer review as the canonical truth-test
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewer who treats peer review as the canonical truth-test misunderstands the institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should be humble about the institution's track record and avoid acting as if their acceptance/rejection decisions are ultimate arbiters of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve work you don't understand for the open community
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should explicitly preserve work they don't understand for the open community rather than discarding it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering novel or difficult-to-evaluate work, avoid dismissing it outright; allow it to be posted and scrutinized publicly so others can replicate, critique, or build upon it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor evidence over consensus or institutional authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Validity depends on evidence, not consensus or institutional authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess manuscripts based on the strength of their evidence, methods, and replicability rather than conformity with prevailing views or prestige of authors/journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support open discourse and reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Science should be an open process where 'anyone can post ideas and results for others to replicate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage practices such as preprints, open data, transparent methods, and public discussion so that claims can be independently tested rather than gatekept by a few reviewers or editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gatekeeping that suppresses legitimate inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Mainstream journals can suppress legitimate inquiry (the lab-leak hypothesis is given as a case study of such suppression).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about rejecting or marginalizing controversial or nonconformist ideas solely because they challenge mainstream consensus; consider whether rejection is preventing legitimate lines of inquiry from being pursued and replicated by others.
